volumes.title: Mr Pym of the Attic
volumes.text:
At Number Nine, Candlewick Row, in the town of Emberwick, there lived a ghost named Mr Osbert Pym. He was tall and thin and the colour of a clean window, and he had the best manners on the whole Grey Coast.

Mr Pym never said boo. He thought it a rude thing to say to a person one had not been introduced to. He never rattled chains, because of the noise, and he never walked through a door without knocking first, which is harder than it sounds when your knuckles go straight through the wood.

The house had stood empty for nine winters. Mr Pym kept it nicely. Each evening he drifted from room to room, straightening the pictures and wishing the mice good night. Then he went up to the attic, hung his hat on a moonbeam, and wished for somebody to be polite to.

volumes.title: The Larkspurs Arrive
volumes.text:
One wet Thursday in March a cart stopped outside Number Nine, Candlewick Row, and a family got down from it. There was Mrs Larkspur, who carried a clock. There was Mr Larkspur, who carried everything else. There was Tansy, who was seven, and a baby called Bram, who was mostly blanket.

Up in the attic, Mr Osbert Pym, the ghost of the house, watched through a crack in the floor and was thrown into a dreadful fluster. Company, after nine winters. And nothing dusted.

He longed to go down and say how do you do. But a ghost cannot simply appear in front of people. It startles them, and startling is bad manners. So Mr Pym stayed where he was, wringing his hat, and listened to the lovely noise of boots on his stairs. Somebody dropped a saucepan. He very nearly called out “Bless you.”

volumes.title: A Card in the Frost
volumes.text:
Mr Osbert Pym was a ghost, the politest in Emberwick, and for three days he had been sharing his house on Candlewick Row with a family who did not know he was there. This troubled him. It felt like eavesdropping.

A gentleman, he decided, leaves his card. Mr Pym had no cards. He did have cold fingers. So on the third night he floated down to the landing window, breathed on the glass to chill it, and wrote in the frost with one careful fingertip. It took him until dawn, because he kept rubbing out the wobbly letters and beginning again.

When he had finished, it said: Mr O. Pym. The Attic. At home on Tuesdays. Please do not trouble to knock. Then he read it over and added, smaller, underneath: I hope the stairs have not been creaking. I have spoken to them.

volumes.title: Tansy Writes Back
volumes.text:
Tansy Larkspur, who was seven, found the writing on the landing window before breakfast. Frost had spelled out a calling card from a Mr O. Pym of the attic, and the sun was already nibbling the edges of it.

Tansy was not a girl who screamed. She was a girl who fetched a pencil. She copied the card onto the back of a flour bag, and then she sat on the top stair and wrote an answer in her best joined-up hand. Dear Mr Pym, it said. We are the Larkspurs. I am Tansy. Tuesday is tomorrow. I will come at four o’clock if that is convenient. Do ghosts take tea?

She pushed it under the attic door. On the other side, a ghost who had not had a letter in a very long time read it eleven times, and then went to look for his better hat.

volumes.title: Tuesday at Four
volumes.text:
At four o’clock on Tuesday, Tansy Larkspur climbed the attic stairs of Number Nine, Candlewick Row, carrying two cups of milk on a tray, because nobody would let her have the teapot.

There was a small cough from inside the old wardrobe. Then a knock, from the inside, three polite taps. “Come out,” said Tansy, which is not what people usually say to wardrobes. Out came Mr Osbert Pym, hat first. He was so tall that he had to stoop under the rafters, and Tansy could see the wallpaper roses straight through his waistcoat.

“I do apologise for the view,” said the ghost. “I am afraid I am rather see-through. It is not deliberate.” Tansy said she liked the roses better that way. Mr Pym could not drink his milk, but he held the cup for a whole hour and said it was the nicest he had ever held.

volumes.title: Trouble With Doors
volumes.text:
Mr Osbert Pym, the ghost in the attic of the Larkspurs’ house, had one friend now, a girl of seven named Tansy. He decided to be useful to the whole family.

He began with doors. Whenever a Larkspur came along with full hands, Mr Pym swept the door open and bowed. Nobody but Tansy could see the bow. They saw only a door opening by itself. Mr Larkspur blamed the hinges and oiled every one. Mrs Larkspur blamed the wind and wedged them all with folded paper. Dumpling the cat blamed nobody, but would no longer go upstairs.

“Perhaps,” said Tansy, “you could do something quieter.” So in the evenings Mr Pym went back to straightening the pictures, and at night, when baby Bram grizzled, he hummed an old slow tune by the cradle until the grizzling stopped. Nobody thanked him. He did not mind in the least.

volumes.title: A Call From Mrs Gale
volumes.text:
Not every ghost in Emberwick is a polite one. One blowy night Mrs Henrietta Gale, who haunts the windmill on the marsh road and can be heard doing it from the river, came down the chimney of Number Nine, Candlewick Row, to call on Mr Osbert Pym.

She looked round his tidy attic and sniffed. All these years in the house, and a family downstairs who slept right through till morning! It was a disgrace to the profession. A ghost should moan. A ghost should clank. She clanked for him, to show how, and dust fell out of the rafters.

Mr Pym said that he would try. When she had gone he stood at the top of the stairs, cleared his throat, and called down into the dark: “Woo. If it is not inconvenient.” Nobody woke. Dumpling the cat opened one eye, and shut it again.

volumes.title: The Polite Thing
volumes.text:
Mr Osbert Pym was a ghost who worried, mostly about his manners. In the attic of the Larkspurs’ house on Candlewick Row he found a new worry and could not put it down.

The doors he had opened had cost Mr Larkspur a whole tin of oil. The cat would not use the stairs. And Mrs Gale, the loud ghost from the windmill, had told him that a house with a family in it was no place for a ghost who could not even moan. Perhaps he was simply in the way.

A guest who is in the way, thought Mr Pym, ought to leave before he is asked. That was the polite thing. So he wrote a note in the frost for Tansy, thanking her for the milk, put on his hat, and went out by the front door. He knocked first, out of habit.

volumes.title: Rain at the Bandstand
volumes.text:
A ghost with no house to haunt is a sorry sight, if you can see him at all. Mr Osbert Pym, late of Number Nine, Candlewick Row, spent his first night away under the bandstand in Emberwick’s river gardens. It rained sideways, and the rain went straight through him, which tickled.

He tried to make the best of it. He wished the ducks good evening. He straightened the notice about keeping off the grass. He told himself the Larkspurs would be far more comfortable without doors that opened by themselves.

Back on Candlewick Row, though, nobody was comfortable at all. The pictures had gone crooked, every one. The stairs had started creaking again. And Tansy Larkspur, aged seven, stood on the landing in her nightgown reading a goodbye written in frost, with her chin stuck out the way it went when she had decided something.

volumes.title: The Missing Hum
volumes.text:
On the second night after the ghost left Number Nine, Candlewick Row, baby Bram Larkspur would not sleep. Mrs Larkspur walked him up and down. Mr Larkspur sang, which made things worse. It was Tansy who said what was wrong. “He wants the humming.”

Her parents looked at each other. There had been a humming, low and old-fashioned, every night by the cradle. Each had supposed it was the other. So Tansy told them everything: the frost card, the Tuesdays, Mr Osbert Pym and his see-through waistcoat. Mrs Larkspur sat down on the stairs. Then she got up again and found her best writing paper.

The Larkspur family, said the invitation, request the pleasure of Mr Pym’s company at home, for as long as he likes. Tansy buttoned it inside her coat and went out to look in every polite place she could think of.

volumes.title: Properly Introduced
volumes.text:
Tansy Larkspur found the ghost at the bandstand in the river gardens, sitting on the conductor’s step, wet through in a way that did not show. She held out the invitation. Mr Osbert Pym read it twice, took off his hat, and for a moment could not say anything at all.

They walked home to Candlewick Row together. At the door of Number Nine he hung back. “I have not been introduced,” he said. So Tansy did it properly. “Mother, Father, this is Mr Pym. Mr Pym, my mother and father, and that is Bram.”

Once they had been told where to look, they could see him quite well: a tall gentleman the colour of a clean window, bowing. Mrs Larkspur said they had wondered who kept the pictures so straight. Mr Larkspur shook his hand, or shook the cold air where it was, and meant it.

volumes.title: Boo, By Request
volumes.text:
Mr Osbert Pym still lives in the attic of Number Nine, Candlewick Row, Emberwick, and on Tuesdays he comes down to tea. A chair is set for him between Tansy and the baby. He cannot drink his cup, but he says the steam is excellent, and he holds it until it goes cold, which with Mr Pym does not take long.

He opens no doors now unless asked. He hums to Bram each night, and the pictures have never hung so straight. Dumpling the cat sleeps on the attic stairs.

On Tansy’s eighth birthday she asked for one thing more. Mr Pym turned quite misty with embarrassment, but a guest does not refuse his hostess. He stood up, smoothed his waistcoat, and said it, once, very softly, with a small bow. “Boo.” Everybody clapped. It was, the Larkspurs agreed, the most polite boo ever heard on the Grey Coast.

volumes.title: The Larder Door
volumes.text:
This is the Emberwick Cold Spot Survey, and I am the surveyor, Hector Brindle, aged ten and three-quarters, of 14 Ropewalk. My assistant is my sister Posy, who is five and carries the thermometer because she cried. A cold spot is a place that is colder than it has any business being. Some people say ghosts cause them. I mean to find out, properly, with equipment.

Cold Spot No. 1. Place: our larder, bottom left, by the onions. Equipment: Gran’s jam thermometer, one feather (for draughts), one biscuit (in case a ghost is hungry, which would be evidence). The thermometer went down. The feather blew sideways. Nobody touched the biscuit except Posy.

Finding: there is a gap under the larder door you could post a kipper through. Cause: draught. Ghost: none. I have written EXPLAINED in red. It is a start.

volumes.title: The Third Stair
volumes.text:
Emberwick Cold Spot Survey, kept by Hector Brindle, surveyor, with Posy Brindle, assistant (thermometer). We test cold places for draughts and ghosts and write down which.

Cold Spot No. 2. Place: Emberwick Library, the main staircase, third stair from the bottom. I found it by accident, going up for a book about volcanoes. One stair was like stepping into a pond. The stairs on either side were ordinary. Posy stood on it and said “Ooh” and would not get off. I held up the feather. It hung straight down. No draught at all, not under the stair, not from the window. The thermometer dropped so far that Miss Plumb the librarian came to see what we were doing and stayed to watch.

Finding: none. Cause: unknown. I have put a question mark, in pencil, in case I need to rub it out. Surveyors do not like question marks.

volumes.title: Mr Haddow’s Doorway
volumes.text:
I am Hector Brindle, and this is my survey of the cold spots of Emberwick, with causes. So far: one draught, one question mark.

Cold Spot No. 3. Place: the doorway of Haddow’s fish shop on Quay Street. It is cold enough there to make your knees ache. I did not need the feather. Mr Haddow keeps his fish on a slab of ice as long as a rowing boat, and the cold rolls out of the door like something spilled. He let my sister Posy hold a crab. Finding: ice. Cause: fish. EXPLAINED, in red.

But I must put down one more thing, because a survey has to be honest. When we had walked on as far as the pump, out of reach of the ice, I felt cold on the back of my neck. The feather hung still. I have not given it a number. Yet.

volumes.title: The Footbridge
volumes.text:
Emberwick Cold Spot Survey. Surveyor: Hector Brindle, ten and three-quarters. Assistant: Posy Brindle, five, in charge of Gran’s jam thermometer.

Cold Spot No. 4. Place: the footbridge over the river Ember, in the middle, where you can see the weir. The air comes up off the water, and Gran says it goes through a coat like a needle. The feather blew about properly. EXPLAINED: river.

Except that it was not cold all over. I am sorry to keep doing this. It was colder on my left side than my right, a patch about the size of an open umbrella, and when I changed places with Posy the cold changed places too and stood on my left again. Posy says it likes that side because that is the side my notebook is on. I told her assistants do not have theories. I wrote it down anyway.

volumes.title: Three Times Round
volumes.text:
I am the surveyor of cold spots in Emberwick, Hector Brindle, and today I did an experiment instead of an entry, because suspicions have to be tested.

The suspicion: one cold spot is not staying in its place. It has been behind me at the pump and beside me on the footbridge. So I walked three times round the bandstand, with my sister Posy in the middle holding the thermometer.

First lap, the cold was at my left elbow. Second lap, I ran, and it fell behind, and caught me up at the steps like somebody out of breath. Third lap, I stopped dead. It bumped into me. It was like being walked into by a pillow that had been kept in a cellar. Finding: Cold Spot No. 5 moves. It follows the surveyor. Posy says it is shy. For once I have let the assistant’s theory stand.

volumes.title: Frost on the Biscuit
volumes.text:
Emberwick Cold Spot Survey, by Hector Brindle with Posy Brindle. Most cold spots stay where they are put. No. 5 follows me about, so today we tried to catalogue it properly, in our back yard at 14 Ropewalk, where nobody would stare.

Size: one open umbrella. Height: up to my shoulder. Temperature: like the inside of a letterbox in January. Feather: hangs still, so no draught. Smell: none, or a bit like snow.

Then Posy held out the ghost biscuit. Nothing ate it. But frost grew across the top while we watched, in a pattern like ferns, and in the middle of the ferns there were letters. They were back to front. I held the biscuit up to Gran’s hand mirror and read them. HELLO. Finding: Cold Spot No. 5 can spell. Posy has named it Brr. I have written GHOST, in red, and underlined it.

volumes.title: What Brr Wanted
volumes.text:
My name is Hector Brindle. I survey the cold spots of Emberwick, and one of them, No. 5, is a ghost called Brr who follows me and writes in frost. Brr is the size of an umbrella and cannot be seen, only felt. My sister Posy says Brr is friendly and a bit sad.

Today we asked questions at the bakery window on Oven Street, which steams up nicely. I asked why a ghost would follow a survey. The frost came slowly. LOST. Then, after Posy said please: NO SPOT.

It took the whole window to get the rest. Every cold place in the town belongs to something. The larder has its draught. The fish shop has its ice. The footbridge has the river. Brr had been all round Emberwick looking for an empty one. Finding: Cold Spot No. 5 has no address. A survey can fix that.

volumes.title: Rooms to Let
volumes.text:
Emberwick Cold Spot Survey. Surveyor Hector Brindle, assistant Posy Brindle, and one ghost, Brr, who is a cold spot with nowhere to live. This week we went house-hunting.

First we tried our larder. Brr stayed ten minutes and wrote ONIONS on the butter dish, with the N backwards. Not suitable. Next, Haddow’s fish shop, which is cold already. But Mr Haddow walked through Brr eleven times while serving one customer, and Brr came out looking thin. I cannot see Brr. Posy told me about the thin.

Last we tried the church porch. There is an old cold spot there already, No. 6, EXPLAINED by flagstones. It did not want a lodger. The frost on the boot scraper just said FULL. Finding: three places tried, none taken. Brr walked home on my left side, close, like a dog told off for something it did not do.

volumes.title: The Question Mark
volumes.text:
I am Hector Brindle of the Emberwick Cold Spot Survey, and I have been stupid, and a surveyor ought to write that down too.

Tonight I went back through the notebook. No. 1, the larder: draught. No. 3, the fish shop: ice. No. 4, the footbridge: river. And No. 2, the third stair in the library, with no cause and a question mark in pencil. I asked Brr, our ghost, who was sitting on the end of my bed making the blanket crackle: was that you? The frost came on the window. YES.

Brr had been resting on that stair one afternoon, and I was the first person who ever stopped. Everybody else shivered and went on up. I stood there with a feather and wrote it down. So Brr followed the notebook. Finding: the question mark was a ghost all along. I have not rubbed it out.

volumes.title: Surveyor in Bed
volumes.text:
This page of the Emberwick Cold Spot Survey is written by Posy Brindle, assistant, age five. Hector is telling me the spellings. Hector has a cold. Not a cold spot. A nose one. Gran says he got it standing on bridges.

He has been in bed four days. Brr, who is our ghost and a cold spot, sat on the end of the bed. Then Gran said there was a draught fit to freeze a kettle and laid the draught sausage along the door. Brr thought the sausage was meant for it. So Brr went and sat out on the landing instead, all night.

I took Brr my mitten. In the morning it had frost on it that said THANK. There was not room for YOU. Finding by me: Brr needs a place of its own where nobody puts a sausage. Hector says that is a good finding.

volumes.title: A Word With Miss Plumb
volumes.text:
I am Hector Brindle, surveyor of cold spots, and today the survey did something instead of only writing things down. We went to Emberwick Library, Posy and I and Brr, our ghost, who is a cold spot without a home.

The third stair was an ordinary stair. It had been ordinary ever since Brr left it to follow me. I showed Miss Plumb the librarian the whole notebook, No. 1 to No. 6, and the question mark. She read every page, not hurrying. Then she asked whether the ghost was a quiet one, and Posy said it only writes, and Miss Plumb said in that case it was better behaved than most of her borrowers.

She fetched a card and her good pen. Brr went and stood on the third stair, and the stair went cold as a pond, and the window above it frosted over in ferns.

volumes.title: Survey Closed
volumes.text:
Emberwick Cold Spot Survey, final page. Surveyor: Hector Brindle, eleven next month. Assistant: Posy Brindle, who can now read the thermometer by herself.

Cold spots catalogued: six. Explained: four, being draught, ice, river and flagstones. The other two turned out to be the same one. Resident: one. There is a card pinned beside the third stair in Emberwick Library, in Miss Plumb’s writing. It says: Cold Spot No. 2. Resident. Please mind the step, and say good afternoon.

People do. We go on Saturdays. Posy hangs her mitten on the banister, and I read out the hottest pages of the volcano book, because Brr, our ghost, likes to be horrified. The window always says something. Last week it said HOME, with the E the right way round. Finding: none needed. Survey closed. Friends: one more than when I started.

series.name: Night Watch at the Old Hall

volumes.title: First Night, Twenty-Three Doors
volumes.text:
Night log of Emberwick Old Hall. Kept by Ned Tarrow, watchman, formerly of the Ember ferry. First night.

Nine o’clock. Took over from Miss Vale, the curator, who gave me a lantern, a ring of twenty-three keys and a list of what they fit. The Hall is shut for mending until Midsummer and full of dust sheets. My orders are to walk it every two hours, lock what is open and write down what I find. Eleven o’clock. First round. Twenty-three doors, all sound. Scullery window found unlatched. Latched it.

One o’clock. Second round. I am certain I left the Long Gallery door open behind me to save my knees coming back. Found it shut and locked. I have the only keys. I counted them. Three o’clock. All quiet. A ferryman is used to being the only one awake. Tonight I am not sure I was.

volumes.title: The Warm Teapot
volumes.text:
Night log, Emberwick Old Hall. Ned Tarrow, watchman. Fourth night. Ten o’clock. I have a chair, a stove and a brown teapot in the porter’s room off the kitchen passage. Before the midnight round I set the kettle on the edge of the stove and left the pot empty, meaning to brew when I got back.

Half past midnight. Round done, all doors sound, scullery window latched by somebody before I reached it. Came back to the porter’s room. The tea was made. Poured, too, one cup, the right colour, with the spoon laid across the saucer the way they do in big houses. Still hot. Then I drank it, since letting it go cold would not have explained anything.

Four o’clock. Nothing further. I said “Much obliged” to the passage on my way through. I felt a fool. I would have felt worse not saying it.

volumes.title: The Grey Housekeeper
volumes.text:
Night log of the Old Hall above the river Ember. Ned Tarrow, watchman, ninth night. I have been finding doors locked ahead of me and tea poured. Tonight I saw who does it.

Two o’clock. Top of the back stairs. A woman in grey coming along the passage, with a cap, an apron and a great ring of keys at her waist. The keys swung and made no sound. I could see the lamp bracket through her shoulder. She tried the nursery door, found it fast, and nodded to herself.

Then she saw me. I took my cap off. She looked at my boots, which were muddy, and then at my face, and gave me one short nod, the kind you give a new boy who may or may not do. Then she went through the wall, where I am told there used to be a door.

volumes.title: Corrections in the Margin
volumes.text:
Night log, Emberwick Old Hall, kept by Ned Tarrow. Third week. The Hall has a ghost, a grey housekeeper with a ring of silent keys, and she does my rounds before I can.

Ten o’clock. I am not proud of this entry. Started the round an hour early to get ahead of her. Every door on the ground floor already locked. Went up the front stairs two at a time, at sixty-one, and found the Long Gallery done and the lamp trimmed.

Midnight. Came back to the porter’s room to find this book open on the table. My entry for Tuesday reads “all sound”. Beside it, in brown ink and a small slanting hand, is written: Scullery window. Again. And on last night’s page, against my count of the doors: Twenty-four. You forget the coal hatch. I went and looked. There is a coal hatch.

volumes.title: Forty Years of Keys
volumes.text:
Night log of the Old Hall. Ned Tarrow, watchman. I asked Miss Vale, the curator, whether the Hall had ever had a housekeeper who wore grey and missed nothing. She did not laugh. She brought down a book.

Six in the evening. It is a housekeeper’s day-book, kept by a Mrs Annis Thorne, who ran the Hall for forty years in the old family’s time. Every page is in the small slanting hand that has been correcting my log. Linen counted. Lamps trimmed. Each night ends the same way: Doors seen to. Keys given up to Mr Pellow, all sound. Good night.

The butler took the keys at night, so that the housekeeper could go off duty. But the last page stops at “Doors seen to”. No keys given up. No good night. Ten o’clock. Began my round. I have been thinking about that last page.

volumes.title: The Gallery Window
volumes.text:
Night log, Emberwick Old Hall. Ned Tarrow, watchman. A gale off the Grey Coast tonight. Half past one. I was in the porter’s room when the servants’ bells began to ring. All eleven on the board, though the wires were cut years back. Then one only, over and over: Long Gallery. I ran.

The big end window had burst its catch and was banging wide, with rain driving in across the floor towards the old family’s portraits. The grey housekeeper, Mrs Thorne, who haunts this house and walks my rounds ahead of me, was there already. She can turn a key, but a wet oak shutter is another matter. Her hands went through it. She looked at me, and for once it was not a look for a new boy.

I put my shoulder to the shutter and dropped the bar. Two o’clock. All sound. Portraits dry.

volumes.title: Upstairs and Down
volumes.text:
Night log of the Old Hall above the river Ember, kept by Ned Tarrow. Seventh week. Since the night of the gale the Hall’s ghost and I have come to an arrangement, though neither of us has mentioned it.

Ten o’clock. Mrs Thorne, the grey housekeeper, takes the upper floors. I take the ground floor, the cellars and the coal hatch, which I no longer forget. Midnight. All sound below. I can hear nothing above, but the lamps on the landing are trimmed, so all is sound there too.

Two o’clock. We meet on the half-landing under the big clock. I have taken to bringing the Emberwick paper and reading her the parts a housekeeper might care for: whose chimney wants sweeping, the price of coal. She stands with her hands folded. At the price of coal she shut her eyes, as people do who remember it cheaper.

volumes.title: She Never Sits
volumes.text:
Night log, Emberwick Old Hall. Ned Tarrow, watchman. I share the watch here with a ghost, Mrs Annis Thorne, housekeeper of the Hall in the old days.

Two o’clock. Half-landing. She was late, which she never is, and when she came I could see more of the wall through her than usual. She flickered at the edges like a lamp wanting oil. I set the landing chair for her. She looked at it as I might look at a boat with a hole in. Nine weeks, and I have never once seen her sit.

Four o’clock. I have worked it out, slowly, as I do. In her day-book, every night ended with the keys handed to the butler and a good night. On the last page nobody took them. So she has been on duty ever since. Nobody is built to stand a watch that long.

volumes.title: A Stiff Note
volumes.text:
Night log of the Old Hall. Ned Tarrow, watchman. The Hall’s ghost is its old housekeeper, Mrs Thorne, who was never relieved of her keys and so has never gone off duty. Tonight I tried to mend that and made a mess of it.

Two o’clock. Half-landing. I told her that I was the night watch now, and that she had earned her rest and should take it. I meant it kindly. I said it like a ferryman, which is to say loudly. She drew herself up until her cap was level with the clock. Then she went through the wall.

Three o’clock. A note in this log, in the brown slanting hand: And who would see to the scullery window? Underneath, pressed hard enough to mark the page: Twenty-four doors, Mr Tarrow. You found twenty-three. Four o’clock. She is right. I have not earned the keys yet.

volumes.title: Earning the Keys
volumes.text:
Night log, Emberwick Old Hall, kept by Ned Tarrow. Twelfth week, and a fortnight to Midsummer, when the Hall opens again. Mrs Thorne, the grey housekeeper who haunts it, will not hand over her watch to a man who forgets coal hatches. So I have stopped forgetting.

Nine o’clock. The joiner came by daylight at my asking and fitted a new catch to the scullery window, brass, with a pin. Tonight I latched it and stood back. I believe I heard a sniff. It was not a displeased one.

Midnight to four. Walked the whole Hall, top to bottom, all twenty-four doors, saying each one aloud as I tried it. Nursery, sound. Linen room, sound. Coal hatch, sound. She came behind me the whole way and checked every one after me. She found nothing to correct. Five o’clock. No note in the log. From Mrs Thorne that is high praise.

volumes.title: Midsummer Eve
volumes.text:
Night log of Emberwick Old Hall. Ned Tarrow, watchman. Midsummer Eve. The Hall opens to the town tomorrow. Tonight I did what somebody should have done for Mrs Annis Thorne, the housekeeper, whose ghost has stood watch here for longer than anyone can tell me.

Ten o’clock. Round done together, twenty-four doors. Then I stood on the half-landing under the clock in my good coat, held out my hand, and said the words from her own day-book. “Doors seen to, Mrs Thorne. I will take the keys now. All sound. Good night.”

She stood a long moment. Then she unhooked the ring and laid it across my palm. It weighed nothing and was cold as well water, and for the first time those keys made a sound: one small chime, like a spoon on a cup. She said, “Good night, Mr Tarrow.” Then she went upstairs. By the stairs.

volumes.title: Two Cups
volumes.text:
Night log, Emberwick Old Hall, open again since Midsummer. Ned Tarrow, watchman. First night of autumn. I keep the watch alone, twenty-four doors, and I have not missed the coal hatch since spring.

Midnight. All sound. Looked in at the old housekeeper’s room. Miss Vale has left it as it was: a narrow bed, and a chair by the window that looks down the river Ember. The cushion on the chair had a dent in it. The room was not cold. It was warm, as a room is when somebody has sat there all evening with nothing to do.

Two o’clock. Mrs Thorne, the Hall’s ghost, is off duty, but she has not gone anywhere. Tonight I came back to the porter’s room and the tea was made. Two cups, and a second chair drawn up across from mine. I read out the price of coal.

volumes.title: What a Bump Is For
volumes.text:
Lesson the first, from your Great-Aunt Hush, who has haunted the Mill House on the marsh since before it had a chimney, to Flit, smallest ghost in Emberwick, lately arrived on the autumn mist and given the bakery on Oven Street to look after.

So you have a house of your own, my dear, and you wish to know how to haunt it. We begin with the bump in the night, and with what it is for. It is not for frightening. Any fool can frighten. A bump is company. It tells the one person awake that the dark is not empty and means no harm.

A house that never bumps is a lonely house. People lie awake in it listening to nothing. Your baker, Miss Batch, gets up at three every morning, alone. That is what you are there for. Go gently, and write to me.

volumes.title: Choosing What to Bump
volumes.text:
Lesson the second, Flit, from your Great-Aunt Hush at the Mill House on the marsh. You are a small new ghost with a bakery to haunt, and you have asked what, exactly, one bumps.

Not china. Never china. Not glass, not the clock, not anything with a lid that rolls. A bump should be soft and round and finish quickly. The best things are a floorboard, an empty coal scuttle, the underside of a table and a sack of something. You have flour sacks in that bakery on Oven Street. You are spoiled.

Nudge, do not shove. Think of a cat getting down off a bed in the next room: that is the sound we want. Practise on the sack by the back door. And never bump twice running in a night. Once is company. Twice is mice, and then they send for a terrier.

volumes.title: Ten Past, Never On the Hour
volumes.text:
Flit, my dear, lesson the third. Great-Aunt Hush writing, from the airing cupboard of the Mill House on the marsh, where I do my best thinking. Today, for my small pupil at the bakery in Emberwick: when to bump.

Never on the stroke of midnight. It is showy, and everyone is expecting it. Never while a clock is striking, either. A wasted bump is a sad thing.

The time to bump is ten minutes after somebody wakes. For the first ten minutes they are busy finding their slippers. After that they begin to listen to the quiet. That is your moment. One soft bump, somewhere off to the side, as if the house had turned over in its sleep. Your Miss Batch comes down to her ovens at three. So: ten past three, the flour sack, once. Then leave her be till the loaves are in.

volumes.title: The Stair That Creaks
volumes.text:
Lesson the fourth, from Great-Aunt Hush of the Mill House to Flit, small ghost of Batch’s Bakery on Oven Street. You have your bump. Now we add the creak.

Every staircase has one stair that creaks, and it is a ghost’s business to know which. In my mill it is the fourth from the top. Go up and down yours tonight, lightly, and learn where it lives.

A creak is a slower thing than a bump. A bump says: someone is here. A creak says: and is going up to bed, the same as you. It is the friendliest sound a house can make, if it comes once and goes upward. A creak coming down the stairs is another matter, and we do not do it. I knew a ghost on the Grey Coast who creaked downward all one winter. The family moved to the Lowlands.

volumes.title: The Matter of the Cat
volumes.text:
Flit, this is your Great-Aunt Hush, writing from the Mill House on the marsh with lesson the fifth. You tell me your bakery on Oven Street has a cat, a large pale one called Semolina, who sits and stares at exactly where you are. Cats can see us. Dogs suspect. Hens have no idea.

You must make friends with her before you bump again. A cat who dislikes the ghost will puff up like a chimney brush, and then the baker looks where the cat is looking, and the whole business becomes alarming.

Sit low. Do not loom. Let her come and walk through you; they like the cool of it in a warm kitchen. Then hold your hand behind her ear, where she will feel a small pleasant chill. After three nights she is your partner, and anything you knock, she will take the blame for.

volumes.title: On Spilling the Flour
volumes.text:
Lesson the sixth. Great-Aunt Hush of the Mill House on the marsh, to Flit, small ghost of the bakery on Oven Street, who writes that all is ruined.

You bumped the flour bin instead of the flour sack. The lid rolled, as I said lids do. Twenty pounds went over the floor, Semolina the cat ran through it, and Miss Batch came down at three to a kitchen like a snowfield with paw prints going up the wall. You have been hiding in the bread oven ever since.

Come out of the oven, child. In the winter of the long frost, when I was newer than you, I meant to nudge a footstool and brought down a whole dresser of plates. That is how I know about china. The miller’s wife laughed till she sat down. Yours swept up and went on baking. She is worth haunting well.

volumes.title: The Draught and the Sigh
volumes.text:
Lesson the seventh, Flit, from your Great-Aunt Hush of the Mill House on the marsh, to one small ghost in an Emberwick bakery. You have bumps and a creak. Here are two quiet things for the days when a bump is too much.

The draught first. Pass close by a curtain and let it lift an inch and fall. That is all. It is for summer evenings, and people like it; they say, “Ah, a breath of air at last.”

The sigh is harder. It is not a moan. Moaning is for windmills and show-offs. A proper sigh is the sound a kettle makes just after it is taken off: short, comfortable, finished. Use it once in a month, when your baker sits down at the end of her morning’s work. If you do it well she will sigh too, without knowing why, and feel better for it.

volumes.title: A Bump in Time
volumes.text:
Flit, my dear. Lesson the eighth, from Great-Aunt Hush at the Mill House. Until now I have taught you bumps for company. There is one other kind. You, at your bakery on Oven Street, may need it any morning.

It is the warning bump. If your Miss Batch nods off in her chair with loaves in the oven, and you smell the crusts going from gold to brown, you do not wait for ten past anything. You go to the largest empty tin in the place and you bump it properly. Loud. Once. As if a loaf had fallen off a shelf.

She will start up and say “Mercy, the bread,” and never think of you at all. We are not thanked for this kind. Then be quiet for the rest of the day. A ghost who has been loud once must be twice as soft afterwards.

volumes.title: Salt on the Doorstep
volumes.text:
Lesson the ninth. Great-Aunt Hush of the Mill House writing to Flit, small ghost of Batch’s Bakery in Emberwick, who is downhearted.

You say that since the flour and the tin, Miss Batch has put a line of salt along the back doorstep. You think she wants you gone. Flit, it means she has noticed somebody is there. She does not yet know what sort of somebody.

So tell her. From tonight you will bump the same way every morning: two soft, then one softer, on the flour sack, at ten past three. Yes, I said twice is mice. Three, alike each day, is a name. No creak, no sigh. Do it for a fortnight. A thing that happens alike each day stops being a fright and becomes a habit, and people grow fond of habits. And step over the salt, dear. It does nothing, but it is manners.

volumes.title: The Rolling Pin Answers
volumes.text:
Flit! Your Great-Aunt Hush has read your letter twice at the Mill House on the marsh and is as pleased as a ghost of her age can decently be. This is lesson the tenth, and you have written most of it yourself.

For thirteen mornings you bumped the flour sack at ten past three, two soft and one softer, in your bakery on Oven Street. On the fourteenth, Miss Batch put down her dough, picked up her rolling pin, and knocked on the table. Two, and a little one. Then she said, “Morning, you,” and went on kneading.

That is as good as a haunting gets, child. Now the rule: when they answer, you do not get clever. No tunes, no long speeches in knocks. Answer once, and let that be the whole conversation. Friends who meet at three in the morning do not need much said.

volumes.title: Your Aunt Comes to Look
volumes.text:
Lesson the eleventh was an examination, Flit, and it is over. I, your Great-Aunt Hush, left my Mill House on the marsh for the first time in sixty winters and came down the river Ember on Tuesday’s fog to see how you haunt your bakery.

I sat unseen in the rafters behind the bread paddles. At three Miss Batch came down. At ten past, you gave the flour sack two soft and one softer, and I could not have told them from my own. She knocked back with the rolling pin. The salt was gone from the step. Semolina the cat slept by the oven door and did not turn an ear.

Then I saw the top shelf. A currant bun on a saucer, steaming. A ghost cannot eat a bun. But somebody thought of you, and that is what the steam is for.

volumes.title: When Not to Bump
volumes.text:
The twelfth and last lesson, from Great-Aunt Hush of the Mill House on the marsh to Flit of Batch’s Bakery in Emberwick, who came to me on the autumn mist not knowing a bump from a bang, and who has passed.

One thing remains, the hardest: when not to bump at all. There will be mornings when your Miss Batch comes down humming, with the fire drawing well and the cat on the sill. On those mornings a house needs nothing from its ghost. Sit on the flour sack and listen to the bread rise. Being quiet company is the top of our trade, and few ghosts get there.

I am going back to my airing cupboard. Some misty autumn a ghost smaller than you will turn up on your doorstep, wanting to know how it is done. Tell them what I told you. Gently, Flit. Always gently.
